The garden had forgotten itself. Weeds rose like minor prophets through the cracked flagstone, their sermons of green unheard by anyone who mattered. She walked there in the mornings, before the dew had finished its slow confession to the sun, and she thought about permanence... how it was a word people used to describe things that simply had not ended yet. The roses, once tended by her grandmother's careful hands, now sprawled in gorgeous anarchy. They bloomed without permission. They died without apology. There was something honest in that, she thought. Something that the manicured gardens of her neighbors could never replicate. Perfection, after all, is a kind of silence. And this garden... this magnificent ruin of tangled vine and wayward blossom... it was singing. Not beautifully. Not in tune. But singing nonetheless, the way all abandoned things eventually learn to sing for themselves.
